reference.source: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery / Sabiston Textbook of Surgery
clinicalPearls: Typically present with painless, bright red bleeding on defaecation, often coating the stool or dripping into the pan, with or without a prolapsing lump
Internal haemorrhoids arise above the dentate line and are usually painless, whereas external components below the dentate line are pain-sensitive and hurt when thrombosed
Classified by degree of prolapse: first degree bleed but do not prolapse, second degree prolapse and reduce spontaneously, third degree require manual reduction, and fourth degree remain irreducible
Contributing factors include chronic straining, constipation, a low-fibre diet, pregnancy, and raised intra-abdominal pressure
First-line management is conservative: increased dietary fibre and fluids, stool softeners, and avoidance of straining, which resolves many early cases
Office procedures such as rubber band ligation and injection sclerotherapy treat lower-grade internal haemorrhoids, while haemorrhoidectomy or stapled procedures are reserved for higher grades
Rectal bleeding must not be attributed to haemorrhoids without excluding colorectal cancer and other proximal pathology, especially in older patients or with alarm features
A thrombosed external haemorrhoid causes acute severe perianal pain and a tense tender lump and may be managed conservatively or by evacuation if presenting early
reference.pathophysiology: Haemorrhoids result from abnormal engorgement and downward displacement of the normal anal cushions, which are vascular submucosal structures that contribute to continence. Chronic straining, constipation, and raised intra-abdominal pressure disrupt the supporting connective tissue, allowing the cushions to enlarge, congest, and prolapse. The classical sites are the left lateral, right anterior, and right posterior positions. Bleeding is arteriovenous in origin, giving the characteristic bright red colour. Thrombosis of external components or prolapsed internal haemorrhoids produces acute pain, and long-standing prolapse can cause mucous discharge and pruritus.
additionalInvestigations: Digital rectal examination and proctoscopy to visualise internal haemorrhoids
Rigid or flexible sigmoidoscopy to inspect the distal bowel
Colonoscopy in patients with alarm features, age over threshold, or unexplained bleeding to exclude malignancy
Full blood count if bleeding is chronic or significant to assess for anaemia
redFlags: Rectal bleeding with weight loss, change in bowel habit, anaemia, or a mass suggesting colorectal cancer
Profuse or persistent bleeding causing symptomatic anaemia
Irreducible, strangulated, or gangrenous prolapsed haemorrhoids with severe pain
Perianal sepsis complicating thrombosed or ulcerated haemorrhoids
reference.prognosis: Most haemorrhoids respond to conservative measures or office procedures with good symptom control, though recurrence is possible. Surgical treatment of advanced disease is effective but may cause post-operative pain and, rarely, incontinence or stenosis.
pitfalls: Attributing rectal bleeding to haemorrhoids without excluding colorectal malignancy
Missing an anal fissure as the cause of painful bleeding
Aggressive banding or surgery in patients with portal hypertension or coagulopathy
Overlooking thrombosis or strangulation as the cause of acute severe pain
references: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
management: First-line management is conservative with increased dietary fibre and fluids, bulk-forming laxatives or stool softeners, and avoidance of straining and prolonged toileting
Use short-course topical preparations for symptomatic relief of pain and irritation
Treat lower-grade internal haemorrhoids with office procedures such as rubber-band ligation or injection sclerotherapy
Reserve haemorrhoidectomy or stapled haemorrhoidopexy for higher-grade, recurrent, or irreducible disease
Manage an acutely thrombosed external haemorrhoid with analgesia and stool softening, considering early excision if seen within the first few days
Exclude colorectal malignancy with colonoscopy in patients with alarm features or unexplained bleeding before attributing bleeding to haemorrhoids
Check a full blood count for anaemia when bleeding is chronic or heavy
